In mathematics, an '''Artin–Schreier curve''' is a [[plane curve]] defined over an algebraically closed field of characteristic <math>p</math> by an equation
:<math>y^p - y = f(x)</math>
for some [[rational function]] <math>f</math> over that field.

One of the most important examples of such curves is [[hyperelliptic curve]]s in characteristic 2, whose [[Jacobian variety|Jacobian varieties]] have been suggested for use in [[Hyperelliptic curve cryptography|cryptography]].<ref>{{cite journal |last= Koblitz |first= Neal | date= 1989 |title= Hyperelliptic cryptosystems |journal= Journal of Cryptology |volume= 1|issue= 3|pages=139–150 |doi= 10.1007/BF02252872}}</ref> It is common to write these curves in the form
:<math>y^2 + h(x) y = f(x)</math>
for some polynomials <math>f</math> and <math>h</math>.

== Definition ==
More generally, an ''Artin-Schreier curve'' defined over an [[algebraically closed field]] of characteristic <math>p</math> is a [[branched covering]]
:<math>C \to \mathbb{P}^1</math>
of the projective line of degree <math>p</math>. Such a cover is necessarily [[Abelian extension|cyclic]], that is, the [[Galois group]] of the corresponding [[algebraic function field]] extension is the [[cyclic group]] <math>\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}</math>. In other words, <math>k(C)/k(x)</math> is an [[Artin–Schreier extension]].

The fundamental theorem of [[Artin–Schreier theory]] implies that such a curve defined over a field <math>k</math> has an affine model
:<math>y^p - y = f(x)</math>
for some rational function <math>f \in k(x)</math> that is not equal to <math>z^p - z</math> for any other rational function <math>z</math>. In other words, if for <math>z \in k(x)</math> we define the rational function <math>g(z) = z^p - z</math>, then we require that <math>f \in k(x) \backslash g(k(x))</math>.

==Ramification==
Let <math>C: y^p - y = f(x)</math> be an Artin–Schreier curve.
Rational function <math>f</math> over an algebraically closed field <math>k</math> has [[partial fraction decomposition]]
:<math>f(x) = f_\infty(x) + \sum_{\alpha \in B'} f_\alpha\left(\frac{1}{x-\alpha}\right)</math>
for some finite set <math>B'</math> of elements of <math>k</math> and corresponding non-constant polynomials <math>f_\alpha</math> defined over <math>k</math>, and (possibly constant) polynomial <math>f_\infty</math>.
After a change of coordinates, <math>f</math> can be chosen so that the above polynomials have degrees coprime to <math>p</math>, and the same either holds for <math>f_\infty</math> or it is zero. If that is the case, we define
:<math>B = \begin{cases} B' &\text{ if } f_\infty = 0, \\ B'\cup\{\infty\} &\text{ otherwise.}\end{cases}</math>
Then the set <math>B \subset \mathbb{P}^1(k)</math> is precisely the set of branch points of the covering <math>C \to \mathbb{P}^1</math>.

For example, Artin–Schreier curve <math>y^p - y = f(x)</math>, where <math>f</math> is a polynomial, is ramified at a single point over the projective line.

Since the degree of the cover is a prime number, over each branching point <math>\alpha \in B</math> lies a single ramification point <math>P_\alpha</math> with corresponding different exponent (not to confused with the ramification index) equal to
:<math>d(P_\alpha) = (p - 1)\big(\deg(f_\alpha) + 1\big) + 1.</math>

==Genus==
Since <math>p</math> does not divide <math>\deg(f_\alpha)</math>, ramification indices <math>e(P_\alpha)</math> are not divisible by <math>p</math> either. Therefore, the [[Riemann–Roch theorem]] may be used to compute that the genus of an Artin–Schreier curve is given by
:<math>g = \frac{p-1}{2} \left( \sum_{\alpha\in B} \big(\deg(f_\alpha) + 1\big) - 2 \right).</math>

For example, for a hyperelliptic curve defined over a field of characteristic <math>p = 2</math> by equation <math>y^2 - y = f(x)</math> with <math>f</math> decomposed as above,
:<math>g = \sum_{\alpha\in B} \frac{\deg(f_\alpha) + 1}{2} - 1.</math>

==Generalizations==
''Artin–Schreier'' curves are a particular case of plane curves defined over an algebraically closed field <math>k</math> of characteristic <math>p</math> by an equation
:<math>g(y^p) = f(x)</math>
for some [[separable polynomial]] <math>g \in k[x]</math> and rational function <math>f \in k(x) \backslash g(k(x))</math>. Mapping <math>(x, y) \mapsto x</math> yields a covering map from the curve <math>C</math> to the projective line <math>\mathbb{P}^1</math>. Separability of defining polynomial <math>g</math> ensures [[Separable extension|separability]] of the corresponding function field extension <math>k(C)/k(x)</math>. If <math>g(y^p) = a_{m} y^{p^m} + a_{m - 1} y^{p^{m-1}} + \cdots + a_{1} y^p + a_0</math>, a change of variables can be found so that <math>a_m = a_1 = 1</math> and <math>a_0 = 0</math>. It has been shown <ref>{{cite journal |last= Sullivan |first= Francis J. | date= 1975 |title= p-Torsion in the class group of curves with too many automorphisms |journal=Archiv der Mathematik |volume= 26|issue=1 |pages=253–261 |doi= 10.1007/BF01229737}}</ref> that such curves can be built via a sequence of Artin-Schreier extension, that is, there exists a sequence of cyclic coverings of curves
:<math>C \to C_{m-1} \to \cdots \to C_0 = \mathbb{P}^1,</math>
each of degree <math>p</math>, starting with the projective line.
